notes.topic: Introduction to Linear Algebra: Systems of Equations and Matrix-Vector Multiplication
notes.summary: This lecture introduces linear algebra by examining systems of linear equations through both row and column pictures across two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and higher-dimensional spaces. It demonstrates how to interpret these systems geometrically using intersecting planes and linear combinations of column vectors. Finally, the session explores singular cases where solutions fail and introduces efficient methods for matrix-vector multiplication.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra?
cornell_notes.note: The central problem of linear algebra is solving a system of linear equations. The course starts by examining the normal, nice case where there is an equal number of equations and unknowns, denoted as n equations and n unknowns.

cornell_notes.cue: How are linear equations represented in matrix form?
cornell_notes.note: A system of linear equations can be written compactly in the matrix form A times X equals B. Here, A represents the coefficient matrix arranged in rows and columns, X is a vector of unknowns, and B is the vector representing the right-hand sides.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the row picture of a linear system?
cornell_notes.note: The row picture involves analyzing one equation at a time, where each linear equation represents a straight line in the x-y plane. The solution to the system is the single point of intersection that lies simultaneously on all of the lines.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the column picture of a linear system?
cornell_notes.note: The column picture views the problem by looking at the columns of the matrix rather than the rows. It asks us to find the correct multiples of each column vector so that their linear combination produces the right-hand side vector B.

A linear combination is formed by multiplying individual column vectors by scalar numbers and then adding the resulting vectors together. This is described as the most fundamental operation in the entire linear algebra course.

cornell_notes.cue: How is a linear combination visualized geometrically?
cornell_notes.note: Geometrically, a linear combination of vectors is visualized by placing the vectors head-to-tail in sequence. You start with a scaled version of the first column vector, attach the next scaled column vector to its tip, and arrive at the final resultant vector.

cornell_notes.cue: How is a 3x3 system represented in matrix form?
cornell_notes.note: A 3x3 system of linear equations can be written compactly in matrix form as AX = B, where A is a 3x3 matrix containing the coefficients of the variables, and B is a 3-dimensional vector on the right-hand side. For our specific example, matrix A consists of rows [2, -1, 0], [-1, 2, -1], and [0, -3, 4], while B is the vector [0, -1, 4].

cornell_notes.cue: What is the row picture for a 3x3 system?
cornell_notes.note: In the row picture, each individual linear equation in three dimensions is represented graphically as a plane. When examining two equations, their intersecting planes form a line, and the addition of a third non-parallel plane causes all three planes to intersect at a single unique point representing the solution.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the column picture for a 3x3 system?
cornell_notes.note: The column picture reframes the matrix equation as taking a linear combination of the three column vectors of matrix A, multiplied by the unknowns x, y, and z respectively, to produce the right-hand side vector B. In our example, because the right-hand side vector happened to match the third column vector, the solution was easily found to be x = 0, y = 0, and z = 1.

cornell_notes.cue: How does changing the right-hand side vector B affect the system?
cornell_notes.note: Changing vector B to a new right-hand side—such as one created by adding column one and column two together—changes the specific point of intersection in the row picture. In the column picture, it means we are now trying to produce this new vector B using a different linear combination of the exact same three columns.

cornell_notes.cue: Can we solve AX = B for every right-hand side B?
cornell_notes.note: This is a fundamental algebra question asking whether the linear combinations of our matrix's columns can successfully fill all of three-dimensional space for any arbitrary vector B. For the specific good matrix chosen in this lecture, the answer is yes, making it a non-singular or invertible matrix.

cornell_notes.cue: When does a matrix fail to produce a solution for every B?
cornell_notes.note: A system runs into trouble and fails to cover all of three-dimensional space if the three column vectors all lie within the same plane. If the columns are coplanar—for instance, if one column is just the sum of the other two—their linear combinations will also remain trapped in that single plane, meaning certain right-hand side vectors B cannot be reached.

cornell_notes.cue: When does a matrix system fail to produce a solution for every right-hand side B?
cornell_notes.note: A system fails when the columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane. For instance, if the third column is simply the sum of the first and second columns, it contributes nothing new, meaning all linear combinations remain confined to that single plane. Consequently, any right-hand side vector lying outside that plane is unreachable, resulting in a singular, non-invertible matrix.

cornell_notes.cue: How can we conceptualize nine-dimensional systems with nine columns?
cornell_notes.note: Although impossible to visualize directly, we can pretend to analyze nine vectors with nine components in a nine-dimensional space. Taking their linear combinations allows us to try to hit a target right-hand side vector B. If a random matrix is chosen via MATLAB, it is almost guaranteed to be invertible and non-singular, allowing us to reach every B.

cornell_notes.cue: What happens in higher dimensions if columns are not independent?
cornell_notes.note: If columns are chosen so that they are not independent—such as the ninth column being identical to the eighth column—they contribute nothing new. Instead of filling out the entire nine-dimensional space, their combinations will only fill out a lower-dimensional subspace, such as an eight-dimensional plane inside the nine-dimensional space.

cornell_notes.cue: What is the preferred way to interpret matrix-vector multiplication $Ax$?
cornell_notes.note: The preferred interpretation views matrix-vector multiplication as a linear combination of the columns of matrix A. For example, multiplying a 2x2 matrix by a vector $x$ composed of entries like [1, 2] means taking one of the first column and two of the second column, then adding them together.

cornell_notes.cue: How does the row-based method of matrix multiplication work?
cornell_notes.note: Alternatively, you can multiply a matrix by a vector a row at a time using a dot product. Each row of the matrix multiplied by the vector x yields a component of the resulting vector, which matches the outcome obtained via the column combination method.

mcqs.question: What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra introduced in the lecture?
options: Finding eigenvalues of a matrix
Solving a system of linear equations
Inverting a non-square matrix
Calculating determinants of high-dimensional arrays
mcqs.answer: Solving a system of linear equations

mcqs.question: In the matrix equation A X = B, what does A represent?
options: The vector of unknowns
The right-hand side vector
The coefficient matrix
The inverse transformation

mcqs.question: How is the row picture defined for a two-by-two system of linear equations?
options: A combination of column vectors meeting at the origin
One equation at a time, where lines meet at a solution point
A rectangular array of numbers representing coefficients
A set of parallel lines with no intersection
mcqs.answer: One equation at a time, where lines meet at a solution point

mcqs.question: What is considered the most fundamental operation in the linear algebra course?
options: Matrix multiplication
Finding a linear combination
Calculating cross products
Row reduction to echelon form

mcqs.question: In the row picture for a 3x3 system of linear equations, what does each individual equation represent geometrically in three-dimensional space?
options: A line
A plane
A point
A sphere

mcqs.question: How is the matrix equation AX = B interpreted in the column picture?
options: As finding the slopes of three intersecting lines
As finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A to produce vector B
As inverting the right-hand side vector into a diagonal matrix
As finding the determinant of the three-dimensional space
mcqs.answer: As finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A to produce vector B

mcqs.question: What makes a matrix 'good', non-singular, or invertible in the context of solving AX = B for every right-hand side B?
options: Its columns all lie in the exact same plane
Its linear combinations of columns fill all of three-dimensional space
All of its entries are strictly positive integers
The right-hand side vector B is always a zero vector
mcqs.answer: Its linear combinations of columns fill all of three-dimensional space

mcqs.question: Under what condition will a 3x3 matrix fail to produce a solution for every possible right-hand side vector B?
options: When the three columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane
When the solution vector X has components equal to zero
When the matrix contains no negative numbers
When the row picture consists of three mutually perpendicular planes
mcqs.answer: When the three columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane

mcqs.question: When do the columns of a matrix cause a singular case where some right-hand side vectors B are unreachable?
options: When all the columns lie in the same plane
When every column is orthogonal to the others
When the matrix is generated randomly using MATLAB
When the number of rows exceeds the number of columns
mcqs.answer: When all the columns lie in the same plane

mcqs.question: What happens if you pick a random 9x9 matrix using MATLAB?
options: It will always have identical columns
It will guarantee a non-singular, invertible matrix
It will fail to produce any valid linear combinations
It will restrict all vectors to a two-dimensional plane
mcqs.answer: It will guarantee a non-singular, invertible matrix

mcqs.question: How is matrix-vector multiplication Ax primarily interpreted as a linear combination?
options: As a sum of the rows of A weighted by the entries of x
As a sum of the columns of A weighted by the entries of x
As the cross product of matrix A and vector x
As the inverse of vector x multiplied by each row of A
mcqs.answer: As a sum of the columns of A weighted by the entries of x

mcqs.question: What is the alternative way to compute matrix-vector multiplication row by row called?
options: A cross product
A determinant calculation
A dot product
An elimination step

# Introduction to Linear Algebra: Systems of Equations and Matrix-Vector Multiplication

## Summary

This lecture introduces linear algebra by examining systems of linear equations through both row and column pictures across two-dimensional, three-dimensional, and higher-dimensional spaces. It demonstrates how to interpret these systems geometrically using intersecting planes and linear combinations of column vectors. Finally, the session explores singular cases where solutions fail and introduces efficient methods for matrix-vector multiplication.

## Cornell Notes

| Cue | Notes |
|---|---|
| What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra? *(0:57)* | The central problem of linear algebra is solving a system of linear equations. The course starts by examining the normal, nice case where there is an equal number of equations and unknowns, denoted as n equations and n unknowns. |
| How are linear equations represented in matrix form? *(2:53)* | A system of linear equations can be written compactly in the matrix form A times X equals B. Here, A represents the coefficient matrix arranged in rows and columns, X is a vector of unknowns, and B is the vector representing the right-hand sides. |
| What is the row picture of a linear system? *(1:31)* | The row picture involves analyzing one equation at a time, where each linear equation represents a straight line in the x-y plane. The solution to the system is the single point of intersection that lies simultaneously on all of the lines. |
| What is the column picture of a linear system? *(1:55)* | The column picture views the problem by looking at the columns of the matrix rather than the rows. It asks us to find the correct multiples of each column vector so that their linear combination produces the right-hand side vector B. |
| What is a linear combination? *(9:51)* | A linear combination is formed by multiplying individual column vectors by scalar numbers and then adding the resulting vectors together. This is described as the most fundamental operation in the entire linear algebra course. |
| How is a linear combination visualized geometrically? *(12:21)* | Geometrically, a linear combination of vectors is visualized by placing the vectors head-to-tail in sequence. You start with a scaled version of the first column vector, attach the next scaled column vector to its tip, and arrive at the final resultant vector. |
| How is a 3x3 system represented in matrix form? *(16:41)* | A 3x3 system of linear equations can be written compactly in matrix form as AX = B, where A is a 3x3 matrix containing the coefficients of the variables, and B is a 3-dimensional vector on the right-hand side. For our specific example, matrix A consists of rows [2, -1, 0], [-1, 2, -1], and [0, -3, 4], while B is the vector [0, -1, 4]. |
| What is the row picture for a 3x3 system? *(19:18)* | In the row picture, each individual linear equation in three dimensions is represented graphically as a plane. When examining two equations, their intersecting planes form a line, and the addition of a third non-parallel plane causes all three planes to intersect at a single unique point representing the solution. |
| What is the column picture for a 3x3 system? *(22:04)* | The column picture reframes the matrix equation as taking a linear combination of the three column vectors of matrix A, multiplied by the unknowns x, y, and z respectively, to produce the right-hand side vector B. In our example, because the right-hand side vector happened to match the third column vector, the solution was easily found to be x = 0, y = 0, and z = 1. |
| How does changing the right-hand side vector B affect the system? *(26:27)* | Changing vector B to a new right-hand side—such as one created by adding column one and column two together—changes the specific point of intersection in the row picture. In the column picture, it means we are now trying to produce this new vector B using a different linear combination of the exact same three columns. |
| Can we solve AX = B for every right-hand side B? *(28:03)* | This is a fundamental algebra question asking whether the linear combinations of our matrix's columns can successfully fill all of three-dimensional space for any arbitrary vector B. For the specific good matrix chosen in this lecture, the answer is yes, making it a non-singular or invertible matrix. |
| When does a matrix fail to produce a solution for every B? *(30:34)* | A system runs into trouble and fails to cover all of three-dimensional space if the three column vectors all lie within the same plane. If the columns are coplanar—for instance, if one column is just the sum of the other two—their linear combinations will also remain trapped in that single plane, meaning certain right-hand side vectors B cannot be reached. |
| When does a matrix system fail to produce a solution for every right-hand side B? *(31:06)* | A system fails when the columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane. For instance, if the third column is simply the sum of the first and second columns, it contributes nothing new, meaning all linear combinations remain confined to that single plane. Consequently, any right-hand side vector lying outside that plane is unreachable, resulting in a singular, non-invertible matrix. |
| How can we conceptualize nine-dimensional systems with nine columns? *(32:34)* | Although impossible to visualize directly, we can pretend to analyze nine vectors with nine components in a nine-dimensional space. Taking their linear combinations allows us to try to hit a target right-hand side vector B. If a random matrix is chosen via MATLAB, it is almost guaranteed to be invertible and non-singular, allowing us to reach every B. |
| What happens in higher dimensions if columns are not independent? *(34:45)* | If columns are chosen so that they are not independent—such as the ninth column being identical to the eighth column—they contribute nothing new. Instead of filling out the entire nine-dimensional space, their combinations will only fill out a lower-dimensional subspace, such as an eight-dimensional plane inside the nine-dimensional space. |
| What is the preferred way to interpret matrix-vector multiplication $Ax$? *(36:45)* | The preferred interpretation views matrix-vector multiplication as a linear combination of the columns of matrix A. For example, multiplying a 2x2 matrix by a vector $x$ composed of entries like [1, 2] means taking one of the first column and two of the second column, then adding them together. |
| How does the row-based method of matrix multiplication work? *(37:37)* | Alternatively, you can multiply a matrix by a vector a row at a time using a dot product. Each row of the matrix multiplied by the vector x yields a component of the resulting vector, which matches the outcome obtained via the column combination method. |

## Practice Questions

1. What is the fundamental problem of linear algebra introduced in the lecture?
   - A. Finding eigenvalues of a matrix
   - B. Solving a system of linear equations
   - C. Inverting a non-square matrix
   - D. Calculating determinants of high-dimensional arrays

2. In the matrix equation A X = B, what does A represent?
   - A. The vector of unknowns
   - B. The right-hand side vector
   - C. The coefficient matrix
   - D. The inverse transformation

3. How is the row picture defined for a two-by-two system of linear equations?
   - A. A combination of column vectors meeting at the origin
   - B. One equation at a time, where lines meet at a solution point
   - C. A rectangular array of numbers representing coefficients
   - D. A set of parallel lines with no intersection

4. What is considered the most fundamental operation in the linear algebra course?
   - A. Matrix multiplication
   - B. Finding a linear combination
   - C. Calculating cross products
   - D. Row reduction to echelon form

5. In the row picture for a 3x3 system of linear equations, what does each individual equation represent geometrically in three-dimensional space?
   - A. A line
   - B. A plane
   - C. A point
   - D. A sphere

6. How is the matrix equation AX = B interpreted in the column picture?
   - A. As finding the slopes of three intersecting lines
   - B. As finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A to produce vector B
   - C. As inverting the right-hand side vector into a diagonal matrix
   - D. As finding the determinant of the three-dimensional space

7. What makes a matrix 'good', non-singular, or invertible in the context of solving AX = B for every right-hand side B?
   - A. Its columns all lie in the exact same plane
   - B. Its linear combinations of columns fill all of three-dimensional space
   - C. All of its entries are strictly positive integers
   - D. The right-hand side vector B is always a zero vector

8. Under what condition will a 3x3 matrix fail to produce a solution for every possible right-hand side vector B?
   - A. When the three columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane
   - B. When the solution vector X has components equal to zero
   - C. When the matrix contains no negative numbers
   - D. When the row picture consists of three mutually perpendicular planes

9. When do the columns of a matrix cause a singular case where some right-hand side vectors B are unreachable?
   - A. When all the columns lie in the same plane
   - B. When every column is orthogonal to the others
   - C. When the matrix is generated randomly using MATLAB
   - D. When the number of rows exceeds the number of columns

10. What happens if you pick a random 9x9 matrix using MATLAB?
   - A. It will always have identical columns
   - B. It will guarantee a non-singular, invertible matrix
   - C. It will fail to produce any valid linear combinations
   - D. It will restrict all vectors to a two-dimensional plane

11. How is matrix-vector multiplication Ax primarily interpreted as a linear combination?
   - A. As a sum of the rows of A weighted by the entries of x
   - B. As a sum of the columns of A weighted by the entries of x
   - C. As the cross product of matrix A and vector x
   - D. As the inverse of vector x multiplied by each row of A

12. What is the alternative way to compute matrix-vector multiplication row by row called?
   - A. A cross product
   - B. A determinant calculation
   - C. A dot product
   - D. An elimination step

<details><summary>Answer key</summary>

1. B — Solving a system of linear equations
2. C — The coefficient matrix
3. B — One equation at a time, where lines meet at a solution point
4. B — Finding a linear combination
5. B — A plane
6. B — As finding a linear combination of the columns of matrix A to produce vector B
7. B — Its linear combinations of columns fill all of three-dimensional space
8. A — When the three columns of the matrix all lie in the same plane
9. A — When all the columns lie in the same plane
10. B — It will guarantee a non-singular, invertible matrix
11. B — As a sum of the columns of A weighted by the entries of x
12. C — A dot product

</details>
